claim: Electrically coupled neural networks are found in every major region of the central nervous system.
source: In recent years, research has confirmed that electrically coupled neural networks are found in every major region of the central nervous system (Condorelli et al., 2000; Bennett and Zukin, 2004; Connors and Long, 2004; Hormuzdi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Electrically coupled networks exhibit synchronized rhythmic activity.
source: One common feature of these networks is their synchronized rhythmic activity (Connors and Long, 2004; Bennett and Zukin, 2004; Connors, 2017; Coulon and Landisman, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Synchronized rhythmic activity in electrically coupled networks is correlated with higher brain functions such as states of arousal, awareness, cognition and attention.
source: which has been shown to be correlated with higher brain functions such as states of arousal, awareness, cognition and attention (Ritz and Sejnowski, 1997; Engel et al., 2001; Buzsáki, 2005; Steriade, 2006; Uhlhaas et al., 2009; Wang, 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: The efficiency of electrical synapses is modulated by electrical and chemical activity, similar to chemical synapses.
source: Recently, it has been demonstrated that the efficiency of electrical synapses is modulated by electrical and chemical activity, very much like chemical synapses (O'Brien, 2014; Marder et al., 2017; Coulon and Landisman, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent research

claim: The inferior olive network was among the first electrically coupled networks to be studied in the mammalian brain.
source: The inferior olive network, which was among the first electrically coupled networks to be studied in the mammalian brain, provides primary excitatory input to the cerebellar cortex (Eccles et al., 1966).
evidence: Supported by citation to historical research

claim: The inferior olive network provides primary excitatory input to the cerebellar cortex.
source: The inferior olive network, which was among the first electrically coupled networks to be studied in the mammalian brain, provides primary excitatory input to the cerebellar cortex (Eccles et al., 1966).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The function of the inferior olive network is to generate synchronous activity in olivary neurons.
source: There is a general consensus that the function of this network is to generate synchronous activity in olivary neurons, which provide temporal information for either learning processes, motor execution, sensory predictions or expectations (Llinás and Sasaki, 1989; Lou and Bloedel, 1992; Welsh et al., 1995; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008; Llinás, 2009; De Zeeuw et al., 2011; Ohmae and Medina, 2015; Heffley et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations representing general consensus

claim: Temporal information in the inferior olive is thought to be generated by subthreshold sinusoidal-like oscillations of the membrane voltage.
source: Temporal information is thought to be generated by the subthreshold sinusoidal-like oscillations of the membrane voltage that appear to emerge from an interplay between the membrane properties and network connectivity (Llinás and Yarom, 1986; Lampl and Yarom, 1997; Manor et al., 1997; Loewenstein et al., 2001; Devor and Yarom, 2002b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Oscillatory activity in the inferior olive is governed by chemical synaptic inputs that partially originate in the deep cerebellar nuclei.
source: Recently, this oscillatory activity was shown to be governed by chemical synaptic inputs that partially originate in the deep cerebellar nuclei and modulate the efficacy of the coupling by defining the spatial extent of the electrically coupled network (Lefler et al., 2014; Mathy et al., 2014; Turecek et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent research

claim: The inferior olive is organized in clusters of up to eight neurons whose dendrites are integrated in glomerulus structures.
source: Early work on the morphological organization of the IO indicated that it is organized in clusters of up to eight neurons, whose dendrites are integrated in glomerulus structures (Sotelo et al., 1974)
evidence: Supported by citation to morphological study

claim: Each olivary neuron is anatomically coupled to roughly ten other neurons.
source: This presumed clustered organization has been supported by dye coupling studies showing that each olivary neuron is anatomically coupled to roughly ten other neurons (Devor and Yarom, 2002a; Leznik and Llinás, 2005; Placantonakis et al., 2006; Hoge et al., 2011; Turecek et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to dye coupling studies

claim: Voltage-sensitive dye imaging studies found ensembles of synchronously active neurons corresponding to a cluster size estimation of hundreds of neurons.
source: Physiologically however, the organization of the network has only been addressed in a few voltage-sensitive dye imaging studies which found ensembles of synchronously active neurons corresponding to a cluster size estimation of hundreds of neurons (Devor and Yarom, 2002b; Leznik et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to imaging studies

claim: Spontaneous unitary events were observed in 74.3% of inferior olive neurons.
source: Such events were observed in 74.3% of the neurons (188 out of 253) with an average rate of 0.7 ± 0.6 Hz (calculated in 70 neurons).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements from 253 neurons

claim: Spontaneous unitary events in inferior olive neurons occur at an average rate of 0.7 ± 0.6 Hz.
source: Such events were observed in 74.3% of the neurons (188 out of 253) with an average rate of 0.7 ± 0.6 Hz (calculated in 70 neurons).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements from 70 neurons

claim: Subthreshold events in inferior olive neurons can be divided into two populations: small and large events.
source: The subthreshold events could readily be divided into two populations of small and large events (Figure 1A inset, circles vs. stars), as shown by the amplitude histogram (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B

claim: High-amplitude events have fast kinetics with an average rise time of 1.3 ± 0.3 ms and average half duration of 3.4 ± 0.3 ms.
source: One type (black to gray circles) had a relatively high amplitude (2.4–16.6 mV; average of 7.5 ± 3.1 mV) and fast kinetics (average rise time of 1.3 ± 0.3 ms and average half duration of 3.4 ± 0.3 ms)
evidence: Based on experimental measurements from a representative neuron

claim: Low-amplitude events have slow kinetics with an average rise time of 2.4 ± 0.4 ms and average half duration of 11.8 ± 5 ms.
source: whereas the second type (green circles) had a relatively low amplitude (0.6–1.9 mV; average of 1.17 ± 0.3 mV) and slow kinetics (average rise time of 2.4 ± 0.4 ms and average half duration of 11.8 ± 5 ms).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements from a representative neuron

claim: The two types of events are unlikely to represent signals arising from different locations along the cell's morphological structure.
source: Plotting the duration as a function of the rise time (Figure 1G), which further supports the two-type scheme, failed to demonstrate a monotonous relationship between the rise-time and half-width that is expected from different dendritic locations of synapses (Rall's cable theory; Rall, 1967). Thus, it seems unlikely that the two types represent signals arising from different locations along the cell's morphological structure.
evidence: Based on analysis of experimental data in Figure 1G and comparison to theoretical expectations from cable theory

claim: In a population of 63 neurons, high-amplitude events had a fast rise time (0.8–2.8 ms; average of 1.4 ± 0.4 ms) and short duration (2.5–8.3 ms; average of 4.2 ± 1.3 ms).
source: The distribution of rise-time and half-width in a population of 63 neurons (of which 49 neurons had the two types of events), which is summarized in Figure 1H–J, confirms that there were indeed two distinct types of events. Whereas the high-amplitude events had a fast rise time (0.8–2.8 ms; average of 1.4 ± 0.4 ms) and short duration (2.5–8.3 ms; average of 4.2 ± 1.3 ms)
evidence: Based on experimental measurements from 63 neurons shown in Figure 1H-J

claim: In a population of 63 neurons, low-amplitude events had a longer rise time (1.3–4.3 ms; average of 2.5 ± 0.6 ms) and a longer duration (3.6–21 ms; average of 12.7 ± 3.9 ms).
source: the low-amplitude events had a longer rise time (1.3–4.3 ms; average of 2.5 ± 0.6 ms) and a longer duration (3.6–21 ms; average of 12.7 ± 3.9 ms).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements from 63 neurons

claim: The frequency of slow events was four times higher than that of fast events.
source: Overall, the frequency of slow events was four times higher (0.56 ± 0.62 Hz; n = 69 neurons) than that of the fast events (0.14 ± 0.18 Hz; n = 58 neurons).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements from 69 and 58 neurons respectively

claim: The shape of slow events is unaffected by DC current injection.
source: Normalizing the event amplitudes (Figure 2A–B, right panels) shows that whereas the shape of the slow events was unaffected by the current injection (A), the fast events showed a slowdown of the late repolarizing phase with hyperpolarization (B).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Fast events show a slowdown of the late repolarizing phase with hyperpolarization.
source: Normalizing the event amplitudes (Figure 2A–B, right panels) shows that whereas the shape of the slow events was unaffected by the current injection (A), the fast events showed a slowdown of the late repolarizing phase with hyperpolarization (B).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: DC current injection has no effect on the amplitude of either slow or fast events.
source: Quantifying the effect of the injected current (see Materials and methods) on the amplitude and duration at 20% of the amplitude in 16 neurons revealed no effect on the amplitude of either type of events (Figure 2C,D; R2 = 0.0057 and 0.0035, respectively).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements from 16 neurons shown in Figure 2C,D

claim: DC current injection significantly increases the duration of fast events.
source: In contrast, DC current injection significantly increased the duration of the fast events (Figure 2F; R2 = 0.712; one-sample t-test p=0.0005).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F

claim: The frequency of slow events remains unaffected by DC current injection.
source: Whereas the frequency of the slow events remained unaffected (Figure 3G, R2 = 0.012), the frequency of the fast events increased by a factor of up to 5 (Figure 2H; R2 = 0.836).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 3G (likely Figure 2G based on context)

claim: The frequency of fast events increases by a factor of up to 5 with DC current injection.
source: Whereas the frequency of the slow events remained unaffected (Figure 3G, R2 = 0.012), the frequency of the fast events increased by a factor of up to 5 (Figure 2H; R2 = 0.836).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 2H

claim: Neither slow nor fast events represent chemical synaptic potentials.
source: Since the membrane potential did not change the amplitude of the events, it implies that neither of them represents chemical synaptic potentials.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observation that membrane potential does not affect event amplitude

claim: Application of excitatory synaptic blockers (DNQX and APV) completely eliminated the presence of fast events.
source: However, application of excitatory synaptic blockers (DNQX and APV) completely eliminated the presence of the fast events (frequency before application was 0.056 ± 0.066 Hz, with zero events after application in n = 5 cells).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements from 5 cells

claim: Fast events likely reflect intrinsic regenerative response that is triggered by excitatory synaptic input.
source: Thus, it is likely that the fast events reflect intrinsic regenerative response that is triggered by excitatory synaptic input (as for the effect on slow events, see below).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations including effects of synaptic blockers

claim: Post-junctional responses to both spontaneous and evoked action potentials in one neuron are precisely correlated with depolarizing events in the coupled neuron.
source: Whole-cell recordings from pairs of coupled olivary neurons revealed that the post-junctional responses to both spontaneous (Figure 3A) and evoked (Figure 3B) action potentials in one neuron were precisely correlated with depolarizing events in the coupled neuron.
evidence: Based on experimental paired recordings shown in Figure 3A and 3B

claim: Post-junctional events in paired recordings resemble spontaneously recorded slow events.
source: Both the spontaneous and the evoked events resembled the spontaneously recorded slow events depicted in Figure 1.
evidence: Based on comparison of experimental data from paired recordings to data in Figure 1

claim: Post-junctional events in paired recordings have an amplitude of 1.2 ± 0.12 mV, a rise time of 3.7 ± 0.9 ms and a duration of 14.9 ± 4.0 ms.
source: These events had an amplitude of 1.2 ± 0.12 mV, a rise time of 3.7 ± 0.9 ms and a duration of 14.9 ± 4.0 ms, thus well within the range of spontaneously measured slow events.
evidence: Based on experimental measurements from paired recordings

claim: In paired recordings from 30 neurons, the amplitudes of post-junctional events varied from 0.12 to 1.40 mV with an average of 0.61 ± 0.35 mV.
source: Paired recordings from 30 neurons showed that the amplitudes of the events varied from 0.12 to 1.40 mV (average of 0.61 ± 0.35 mV) whereas the average rise times and half durations were 2.61 ± 1.09 ms and 14.31 ± 6.72 ms, respectively
evidence: Based on experimental measurements from 30 paired recordings

claim: The shapes of evoked synaptic events differ significantly from those of spontaneous slow events.
source: The shapes of the evoked synaptic events differed significantly from those of the spontaneous slow events in the same neurons (p<0.002 for all comparisons (rise time, half duration and amplitudes), paired t-test, n = 17 cells)
evidence: Based on experimental measurements with statistical analysis from 17 cells

claim: The small and slow spontaneous events represent action potentials occurring in electrically coupled neurons.
source: This strongly suggests that the small and slow spontaneous events represent action potentials occurring in electrically coupled neurons.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental comparisons of different event types

claim: Chemical synaptic blockers drastically reduced the frequency of slow events from 2.27 ± 1.75 Hz to 0.068 ± 0.078 Hz.
source: The chemical synaptic blockers drastically reduced the frequency of the slow events (from 2.27 ± 1.75 Hz to 0.068 ± 0.078 Hz) while amplitude, rise time and duration at half amplitude were not affected (p=0.8, 0.25 and 0.96 respectively; paired KS test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements with statistical analysis

claim: The slow events represent the post-junctional responses to action potentials in coupled cells.
source: We conclude that the slow events represent the post-junctional responses to action potentials in coupled cells and therefore we refer to them as 'spikelets'.
evidence: Based on synthesis of multiple experimental observations

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between the coupling coefficient and the spike coupling coefficient.
source: As shown in Figure 3C, there was a significant positive correlation (with a slope of 0.134; R2 = 0.614, p<0.0001; Pearson correlation).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: About 50% of olivary neurons show spontaneous subthreshold oscillations.
source: About 50% of the olivary neurons showed spontaneous subthreshold oscillations (Figure 3E).
evidence: Based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3E

claim: The peaks of subthreshold oscillations are crowned with spikelets.
source: Careful examination of the peaks of the oscillations (Figure 3F) revealed that they were crowned with spikelets.
evidence: Based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3F

claim: The autocorrelation function of subthreshold oscillations matches the inter-spikelet-interval distribution.
source: To quantify this observation, we calculated the distribution of the inter-spikelet-interval (ISLI, Figure 3G, black bars), and found distinct groups appearing at intervals of 200 ms. We then calculated the autocorrelation function of the subthreshold oscillations (Figure 3G, yellow line) and found that it matched the ISLI perfectly.
evidence: Based on experimental analysis shown in Figure 3G

claim: In non-oscillating neurons, the inter-spikelet-interval exhibits a Poisson-like distribution.
source: It is important to note that a similar fit was observed in 60% of the oscillating neurons (n = 18) whereas in non-oscillating neurons (n = 70) the ISLI exhibited a Poisson-like distribution (Figure 3H).
evidence: Based on experimental observations from 70 non-oscillating neurons shown in Figure 3H

claim: The strong correlation between oscillatory behavior and the occurrence of spikelets supports the conclusion that these events represent activity in adjacent electrically coupled neurons.
source: The strong correlation between oscillatory behavior and the occurrence of spikelets further supports the conclusion that these events represent activity in adjacent electrically coupled neurons.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations of correlation between oscillations and spikelets

claim: Common spikelets represent action potentials in additional neurons that are coupled to both recorded neurons.
source: Since action potentials in one neuron evoke very similar spikelets in the other (Figure 3A–B), the most likely explanation is that each of these common spikelets represents the action potential in an additional neuron that is coupled to both of the recorded neurons (see Discussion).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations in paired recordings

claim: 18 out of 30 pairs (60%) had common spikelets.
source: On the population level, 18 out of 30 pairs had common spikelets (60%).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements from 30 paired recordings

claim: The occurrence of common spikelets varied from 0.02 to 1.1 Hz, which is 3.5–66% of the total number of measurable spikelets.
source: Of these pairs, the occurrence of common spikelets varied from 0.02 to 1.1 Hz, which is 3.5–66% of the total number of measurable spikelets (Figure 4D).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 4D

claim: A neuron can connect to as many as 40 other neurons with an average of 19.2 ± 10.3.
source: This analysis was performed on 18 dual recordings and the results, which are summarized in Figure 4F, indicate that a neuron can connect to as many as 40 other neurons (average of 19.2 ± 10.3).
evidence: Based on analysis of experimental data from 18 dual recordings shown in Figure 4F

claim: The use of a slice preparation contributed to the wide range of connected neurons and to some degree of underestimation.
source: It should be noted that the use of a slice preparation undoubtedly contributed to the wide range of connected neurons and to some degree of underestimation (see Discussion).
evidence: Based on inference about experimental limitations

claim: The approach to estimate the number of connections per neuron provides a reliable estimate of the mean number of connected cells.
source: However, the estimation of the mean number of connected cells (+ sign in Figure 5D) is less sensitive to simulation duration or to variability in firing rate (Figure 5F, see discussion). We conclude that this approach provides a reliable estimate of the mean number of connected cells.
evidence: Based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 5D and 5F

claim: The number of common groups varied from 0 to 7 with a markedly higher incidence at 2–4 groups.
source: The number of common groups (Figure 6B) varied from 0 to 7 with a markedly higher incidence at 2–4 groups.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: A simple distance-dependent network fails to reproduce the distribution of common spikelet groups found experimentally.
source: As shown in Figure 6C–E, the simple distance-dependent network captured the distance-dependent probability of a connection (Figure 6D, p=0.99, for detailed statistical analysis see Materials and methods and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), but it failed to reproduce the distribution of common spikelet groups as found experimentally (Figure 6E, p<0.002, Fisher's Exact).
evidence: Based on computational modeling with statistical comparison to experimental data

claim: When the modeled network is organized in clusters, it replicates both the experimental distribution of common groups and the distance-dependent connection probability.
source: On the other hand, when the modeled network was organized in clusters, it replicated both the experimental distribution of common groups (Figure 6H, p=0.13) and the distance-dependent connection probability (Figure 6G, p=0.96).
evidence: Based on computational modeling with statistical comparison to experimental data shown in Figure 6G and 6H

claim: The inferior olive is not connected with a simple distance-dependent rule; instead it is more likely organized into clusters of neurons.
source: Thus, we show that the IO is not connected with a simple distance-dependent rule; instead it is more likely that it is organized into clusters of neurons with a higher probability of connection within clusters and a low connection probability between clusters.
evidence: Based on synthesis of computational modeling and experimental data comparisons

claim: There are two populations of unitary events in inferior olive neurons that differ in their waveform and amplitude.
source: We showed that there are two populations of unitary events that differ in their waveform and amplitude.
evidence: Based on experimental observations and analysis

claim: Spikelets represent the occurrence of action potentials in a coupled neuron.
source: The spikelets represent the occurrence of action potentials in a coupled neuron, while the fast events are likely to represent intrinsic regenerative responses at remote locations.
evidence: Based on synthesis of experimental observations

claim: Fast events are likely to represent intrinsic regenerative responses at remote locations.
source: The spikelets represent the occurrence of action potentials in a coupled neuron, while the fast events are likely to represent intrinsic regenerative responses at remote locations.
evidence: Based on synthesis of experimental observations

claim: Each olivary neuron is connected to approximately 20 other neurons.
source: Analysis of the experimental results showed that each olivary neuron is connected to ~20 other neurons
evidence: Based on analysis of experimental data from paired recordings

claim: The inferior olive network is organized into clusters of neurons, where the probability of connection within a cluster is higher than the probability of connection between clusters.
source: and theoretical considerations indicated that the neurons are not connected in a simple distance-dependent manner, rather that the network is organized into clusters of neurons, where the probability of connection within a cluster is higher than the probability of connection between clusters.
evidence: Based on computational modeling and comparison to experimental data

claim: A single olivary cell by itself cannot oscillate, whereas in a network formation the neurons generate subthreshold oscillations.
source: Thus, a single cell by itself cannot oscillate, whereas in a network formation the neurons generate subthreshold oscillations (Manor et al., 1997; Loewenstein et al., 2001; Chorev et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: When the recorded cell is oscillating, the entire network is synchronously oscillating.
source: Therefore, when the recorded cell is oscillating, the entire network is synchronously oscillating, thus generating action potentials at the peak of the oscillation that appear in the recorded cell as spikelets.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations of correlation between oscillations and spikelets

claim: This constitutes the first physiological study that supports the assumption of clustered organization of the inferior olive nucleus deduced mainly from morphological studies.
source: Although the size of the clusters, as well as the probability of connection cannot be defined with the current data, this constitutes the first physiological study that supports the assumption of clustered organization of the nucleus deduced mainly from morphological studies.
evidence: Based on comparison of current physiological findings to prior morphological studies

claim: The approach to analyze electrically coupled networks should not be restricted to the inferior olive network.
source: This approach to analyze electrically coupled networks should not be restricted to the inferior olive network.
evidence: Based on speculation about broader applicability of the method

claim: Spontaneous spikelets are readily observed in paired recordings from many electrically coupled networks in the central nervous system.
source: Most of the studies on electrical coupling in central neurons used paired recordings, an essential procedure to demonstrate electrical coupling. In many of these recordings spontaneous spikelets are readily observed.
evidence: Based on general knowledge of the literature on electrically coupled networks

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the Hebrew University's Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the Hebrew University's Animal Care and Use Committee.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval

claim: Brain stem slices were prepared from C57BL/6, B6.Cg-Tg (Thy1-COP4/EYFP), and Gad2-tm2(cre)Zjh/J strains of mice.
source: Brain stem slices were prepared from the following strains of mice: C57BL/6, B6.Cg-Tg (Thy1-COP4/EYFP; Jackson Laboratory) and Gad2-tm2(cre)Zjh/J (Jackson Laboratory).
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: 300 µm coronal brainstem slices containing the inferior olive were dissected.
source: Mice were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of Pentobarbital (60 mg/Kg), and 300 µm coronal brainstem slices containing the inferior olive were dissected using a Campden 700smz slicer (Campden Instruments)
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: Recordings were targeted to the deepest neurons possible in the slice to record from intact olivary networks.
source: In order to record from intact olivary networks, recordings were targeted to the deepest neurons possible in the slice.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: For pair recordings, two cells located up to 50 µm apart were selected.
source: For pair recordings, two cells located up to 50 µm apart were selected.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: The coupling coefficient was calculated as the ratio between the change in the steady-state voltage of the post-junctional cell and that of the pre-junctional cell in response to 250 ms current injection.
source: The coupling coefficient (CC, Figure 3C) was calculated as the ratio between the change in the steady-state voltage of the post-junctional cell and that of the pre-junctional cell in response to 250 ms current injection in the pre-junctional cell.
evidence: Description of analysis methods

claim: Common spikelets were defined as spikelets detected in both cells within a time window of 8 msec.
source: Common spikelets were defined as spikelets that were detected in a paired recording in both cells simultaneously. To that end, we searched for spikelets which peaks occurred in both cells within a time window of 8 msec.
evidence: Description of analysis methods

claim: Three olivary neurons were reconstructed from fluorescence image stacks using Neurolucida software.
source: Using the Neurolucida software (MBF Bioscience), three olivary neurons were reconstructed from fluorescence image stacks acquired using a Leica TCS SP5 confocal microscope (Leica Microsystems).
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: A compartmental model was generated from the morphological reconstruction using NEURON.
source: A compartmental model was generated from the morphological reconstruction using NEURON (Carnevale and Hines, 2006).
evidence: Description of modeling methods with citation

claim: The modeled network was composed of 1134 neurons randomly distributed within a volume of 250 × 500×200 µm.
source: We constructed a network of IO composed of 1134 neurons randomly distributed within a volume of 250 × 500×200 µm, which resulted in 0.045 neurons per 10 µm3.
evidence: Description of modeling methods

claim: The probability of a connection between two neurons decays with distance according to a Gaussian profile.
source: The probability of a connection between two neurons decays with distance according to a Gaussian profile
evidence: Description of modeling approach
